They are composed of an ophitic groundmass of labradorite or bytownite feldspar surrounding pseudomorphs of sericite, chlorite and ores after olivine and augite; vesicles are filled with hydrothermal epidote, calcite, chalcedony or chlorite. The Jotnian sequence is extensively cut by (‘post-Jotnian’) dolerites mostly in the form of sills and thick SE-NW dykes; these are fresh ophitic dolerites comprising labradorite feldspar, augite, olivine, ilmenite and magnetite. Under favourable circumstances these may yield essen- tially instantaneous records of the geomagnetic field and (in the latter case) place this informa- tion in a time sequence. Real progress in under- standing the Precambrian geomagnetic field is hampered by the paucity of suitable volcanic andlor sedimentary suites. Studies to date on the ca. 1100 Ma Keweenawan lavas of North America (eg. Thermal demagnetization In thermal demagnetization the rock samples were heated in steps to progressi­ vely higher temperatures and cooled to room temperature after each heating step in a zero field. After the cooling the intensity and the direction of the re­ maining magnetization was measured. Thermal demagnetization is based on destroying the remanent magnetiza­ tion of particles with blocking temperatures lower than the selected heating temperature. During the cooling, in a zero field, the domains in the particles acquire a random magnetization. The net effect of this random magnetization for the remanence is zero. In contrast to the alternating field demagnetizing method the thermal effects have no preferential direction. In the alternating field demagnetizing method, in which an alternating field of a certain strength is applied successively along three perpendicular axes, the maximum effect occurs in the domains with a magnetic moment directed parallel to the demagnetization axes. Thermal demagnetization In thermal demagnetization the rock samples were heated in steps to progressi­ vely higher temperatures and cooled to room temperature after each heating step in a zero field. After the cooling the intensity and the direction of the re­ maining magnetization was measured. Thermal demagnetization is based on destroying the remanent magnetiza­ tion of particles with blocking temperatures lower than the selected heating temperature. During the cooling, in a zero field, the domains in the particles acquire a random magnetization. The net effect of this random magnetization for the remanence is zero. In contrast to the alternating field demagnetizing method the thermal effects have no preferential direction. Thermal demagnetization In thermal demagnetization the rock samples were heated in steps to progressi­ vely higher temperatures and cooled to room temperature after each heating step in a zero field. After the cooling the intensity and the direction of the re­ maining magnetization was measured. Thermal demagnetization is based on destroying the remanent magnetiza­ tion of particles with blocking temperatures lower than the selected heating temperature. During the cooling, in a zero field, the domains in the particles acquire a random magnetization. The net effect of this random magnetization for the remanence is zero. In contrast to the alternating field demagnetizing method the thermal effects have no preferential direction. In the alternating field demagnetizing method, in which an alternating field of a certain strength is applied successively along three perpendicular axes, the maximum effect occurs in the domains with a magnetic moment directed parallel to the demagnetization axes. Thermal demagnetization In thermal demagnetization the rock samples were heated in steps to progressi­ vely higher temperatures and cooled to room temperature after each heating step in a zero field. After the cooling the intensity and the direction of the re­ maining magnetization was measured. Thermal demagnetization is based on destroying the remanent magnetiza­ tion of particles with blocking temperatures lower than the selected heating temperature. During the cooling, in a zero field, the domains in the particles acquire a random magnetization. The net effect of this random magnetization for the remanence is zero. In contrast to the alternating field demagnetizing method the thermal effects have no preferential direction. In the alternating field demagnetizing method, in which an alternating field of a certain strength is applied successively along three perpendicular axes, the maximum effect occurs in the domains with a magnetic moment directed parallel to the demagnetization axes. Thermal demagnetization In thermal demagnetization the rock samples were heated in steps to progressi­ vely higher temperatures and cooled to room temperature after each heating step in a zero field. After the cooling the intensity and the direction of the re­ maining magnetization was measured. Thermal demagnetization is based on destroying the remanent magnetiza­ tion of particles with blocking temperatures lower than the selected heating temperature. During the cooling, in a zero field, the domains in the particles acquire a random magnetization. The net effect of this random magnetization for the remanence is zero. In contrast to the alternating field demagnetizing method the thermal effects have no preferential direction. In the alternating field demagnetizing method, in which an alternating field of a certain strength is applied successively along three perpendicular axes, the maximum effect occurs in the domains with a magnetic moment directed parallel to the demagnetization axes. So, domains with a magnetic moment 42 F. G. NEUVONEN Institute of Geology, University of Turku, Finland ABSTRACT The direction and strength of remanent magnetization were measured for different intrusive rocks of the Precambrian Åva ring intrusion. Two nearly opposite directions were revealed after demagnetization, both in agreement with earlier measurements in SW-Finland. The pole sites are compared with those measured in Sweden. The pole wandering curve and the reversal periods are considered as tools in the Precambrian stratigraphy. E DOLERITE AND RELATED DIKES IN THE ÅLAND ARCHIPELAGO K. J. NEUVONEN and LEO GRUNDSTRÖM Institute of geology, University of Turku, Finland ABSTRACT The dikes of the area can be divided into three groups having different directions of remanent magnetization after demagnetization in the AC field. One of these groups has a direction which coincides with that measured for the Jot- nian dolerites in the Satakunta and Vaasa archipelago. The direction of the second group differs but slightly from this and the third one has a reversed orientation. The age relations and the origin of the magnetization are discussed. tization during the later history of the rock . There are many different ways in which rocks are remagnetized (see Cox and Doell, 1960). As pointed out by Graham and others (1957), one of the most important ways in which the remagneti­ zation of igneous rocks takes place is magnetostriction - or the magnetizing effect of stress. Quite commonly late chemical changes , like weathering , introduce secondary remanent magnetization in rocks (Nagata, 1961). Bulk remanent magnetization, which is measurable with a sensitive magnetometer, may thus be composed of many components of different origin. Usually , we are interested only in the most primary magnetization of a rock. Fortunately , later magnetization can in some cases be removed by »cleaning» rock specimens by me ans of partial demagnetization. This is possible when the primary magnetization is more stable than the later components. This demagnetization is done in an alternating magnetic field of sufficient strength (Brynjolfsson , 1957; As and Zijderveld , 1958 ; and Creer, 1959), or by heating the specimens in a magnetically zero field to an elevated temperature (Irving and others , 1961; and Chamalaun and Creer 1964). The apices of the diagram represent the three components that mainly account for the observed mineralogical variation within the facies. The af characteristics of this collection are essentially very similar to those reported from other studies of the same rock suite (Poorter 1976; Larson & Magnusson 1976). Also, in studies of Jotnian dolerites from Finland (Neuvonen 1965, 1966) the overall mean direction computed from the af cleaned directions has a steeper negative magnetic inclination than that computed from the total NRM, and reflects the removal of a similar small viscous component to that present in the Swedish dolerites. To determine whether the stable end points defined by the af cleaning relate to the initial igneous episode and reside in single high blocking temperature components, one pilot sample from each site has also been thermally demagnetized at a range of steps up to 525" C. The residual magnetic moments in all samples do not show appreciable fall until temperatures approaching the Curie points, and directions of magnetization remain identical to the af cleaned directions (Fig. 2). It is inferred that the af cleaning treatment has successfully recovered the primary magnetization in these dolerites; the simple behaviour to stages of this treatment is consistent with the opaque mineralogy, as neither maghemite nor hematite have been identified in these rocks (Larson & Magnusson 1976). study of Jotnian dolerites Mulder (1 97 1) considered that they may have been remagnetized in Palaeozoic times but this possibility has been rejected by later authors, notably by Poorter (1976). In addition to the evidence documented by this latter author, the Jotnian dolerites in east Sweden are remote from the Caledonian Front, they have partially remagnetized the older Nordingrl Complex and also have a magnetization quite different from the (Cambrian) Alno Island Alkaline Complex in the same area (Piper, in preparation). From measurements on magnetite concentrates from the Ulvo region (18.7" E, 68.0" N) Larson & Magnusson derived Curie points close to that of pure magnetite. Thermomagnetic determinations on whole rock samples (e.g. Fig. 3) also yield single Curie points in the range 500-575" C with little or no change on heating in air, and suggest that the host magnetite has achieved a composition near to that of pure magnetite by exsolution of ilmenite lamellae (Ade-Hall, Palmer & Hubbard 1971); no hematite has been identified from these investigations. The dolerites (although widely referred to in the literature as 'Jotnian', they should strictly be defined as 'post-Jotnian') have been dated 1245 Ma in central Sweden by the K-Ar isochron method (Welin & Lundqvist 1975), a determination recently confirmed by extensive Rb-Sr studies of Patchett, Byland & Upton (1978). Reheating to this temperature would be expected to cause altera- tion of the dolerite and considerable disturbance to the mineral lines: this does not appear to be the case unless complete isotopic resetting of all minerals, in- cluding apatite and clinopyroxene has taken place without any alteration or textural recrystallisation. Additionally, the biotite from country rock granite 15 km closer to the Front Zone than the Karlshamn dyke shows no evidence of Rb-Sr resetting in Sveconorwegian time, and this does not allow a temperature higher than ca. 300 °C, on the basis of the estimated blocking temperature of Alpine biotites [45]. Thus the Karlshamn result must be regarded as an igneous magnetisation unless it is supposed that an original thermal remanence was completely reset at a temperature lower than 300°C, which seems unlikely. The Karlshamn result and the results for the dolerites in general are therefore taken as representing cooling closely following igneous intrusion, and as the dolerites have ages between 1000 and 900 m.y., then this age can also be assigned to the Sveconorwegian and Front Zone poles, which lie on the same trend (Fig. 4). Since the two polar paths do not correspond, but appear to meet at an approximate Keweenawan age of 1000 m.y., this age assignment implies a convergence between a separate continent "Grenvillia" and the pre-Grenville shield during 1120-1000 m.y., with collision occurring at ca. 1000 m.y. along a hypothetical suture within the Grenville Province [22,23,17,15]. The problem of the history of the Grenville- Sveconorwegian Province, as it concerns palaeomag- netism and related geochronology, is therefore made up of two factors: (1) the ages of the Grenville and Sveconorwegian poles are not independently known, and (2) there is not a complete palaeomagnetic record for the pre-Grenville/Sveconorwegian regions from 1400 to 700 m.y., hence the ages of the Gren- ville and Sveconorwegian poles cannot be approxi- mated by comparison with dated poles. This study discusses Rb-Sr mineral age data and palaeomagnetic poles for dolerites, chiefly dykes which intrude the pre-Sveconorwegian (Svecofennian)region of Sweden;the width of the dykes (or thickness in the case of sills) ranges from 5 to 250 m, and they consist of a variety of olivine- and/or hypersthene-bearing dolerites [28]. The dykes trend consistently parallel to the Sveconorwegian Front or Schistosity Zone which separates the Sveconorwegian Province from the Svecofennian, and occur along almost its whole 700-kin length over a belt up to 150 km in width from the Front eastwards (Fig. 1). Samples from the farsundite body yielding mean unblocking temperatures of 520 and 570°C have palaeopoles separated by an angular distance of 35 ° and imply an a.p.w, rate of 3 ° Ma -1. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. Precambrian Res., 23: 201--246. The Sveconorwegian belt is a broad terrain in the south western sector of the Fenno- scandian Shield subjected to thermal activation, widespread intrusion and limited tec- tonic activ

ile events. This study comprises a palaeomagnetic investigation of four areas spanning the zone: the anorthosite, farsundite and related intrusive complexes of southwest Norway, the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector bordering the Oslo Graben, the gabbro--anorthosite complex at BrattSn and ~,lgSn in west Sweden, and dolerite intrusions near the eastern tectonic front to the zone in Sweden. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. The total swathe represents 10--20 ° of a.p.w, movement at 940--900 Ma; an isolated later ('Y') magnetisation may represent a later extension of the path at ca. 840 Ma. Two sets of magnetisations, a NW negative, predominantly hematite-held, and SSW negative, predominantly magnetite-held, are recognised in the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector and are linked to radiometric events at 1090 and 1010 Ma. In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). This study comprises a palaeomagnetic investigation of four areas spanning the zone: the anorthosite, farsundite and related intrusive complexes of southwest Norway, the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector bordering the Oslo Graben, the gabbro--anorthosite complex at BrattSn and ~,lgSn in west Sweden, and dolerite intrusions near the eastern tectonic front to the zone in Sweden. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. The total swathe represents 10--20 ° of a.p.w, movement at 940--900 Ma; an isolated later ('Y') magnetisation may represent a later extension of the path at ca. 840 Ma. Two sets of magnetisations, a NW negative, predominantly hematite-held, and SSW negative, predominantly magnetite-held, are recognised in the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector and are linked to radiometric events at 1090 and 1010 Ma. This variation is present within single cores, between cores from the same site with different coercivity or blocking temperature spectra, and between areal distributions of sites, and this same feature is clear from regional assessments of palaeomagnetism in the Grenville terrain of the Lau- rentian Shield (McWilliams and Dunlop, 1978; Roy and Blythe-Robertson, 1979). In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). d by basic intrusions. In Sweden, these intru- sions are mostly small lensoid bodies a few metres in width intruded parallel to the regional foliation. They are sparsely distributed through much of the terrain, but are very densely intruded towards, and into, the Schistosity Zone where they range from unaltered dykes with chilled margins to com- pletely amphibolitised bodies in localised shear zones subjected to intense deformation. The intrusions of the Kristineham area (palaeomagnetic sites 175--180) have been described in detail by Wiman (1968); they include olivine-bearing ophitic dolerites containing orthopyroxene, ilmenite and magnetite. There is typically a transition from massive olivine-bearing centres into amphibolitic marginal zones within the individual bodies, such that the ophitic texture is gradually destroyed and the pyroxenes and the olivine are replaced by amphibole. The age of hyperite intrusion is not well known, indeed it is possible that they were intruded during several intervals. Mulder (1971) derived K--Ar ages in the range 1569--786 Ma and Klingspar (1976) dated hyperite dolerites from areas further south in the range 1595--679 with a peak of K--At ages between 1050 and 750; Rb--Sr whole-rock determination on a hyperite yielded an age of 1565 *-

A sampling site comprises a minimum of 7 cores distributed over several metres of outcrop and drilled with a portable drilling motor of the kind de- scribed by Doell and Cox (1967). Cores were orientated by sights on the Sun or, in the limited number of cases where this was not possible, by magnetic bearings in conjunction with topographic sights. The cores were sliced in the laboratory and measured with an automated parastatic magnetometer system. Alternating field (a.f.) demagnetisation is most suitable for analysing the broad range of coercivities present in the (predominantly magnetite-held) remanences in these rocks and was utilised in increments of 5 or 10 mT (milliTesla) as the standard method of treatment for this collection. FISH Department of Geological and Geophysical Sciences, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08540 ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic measurements (including alternating field demagnetization) on 16 oriented samples from five sites in the Precambrian anorthosite massif at Eger- sund, southern Norway, revealed a stable, consistent reversed remanent magnetiza- tion (after 150 oersted AF demagnetization, D = 315°, I = -82°, k = 92, a95 = 8°). The calculated paleomagnetic (south) pole lies at 42° N., 20° E. and is more than 45° from the pole (39° N., 40° W.) previously obtained from anorthosite of similar age at Allard Lake, Quebec. If Eurasia is fitted to North America accord- ing to the model of Bullard and others (1965), the rotated Egersund pole is at 42° N., 18° W. Allowing for the uncertainties in the data, this is not significantly different at the 5-percent level from the Allard Lake pole, and suggests that about 1,000 m.y. ago North America and Europe were contiguous as in Laurasian recon- structions. FISH Department of Geological and Geophysical Sciences, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08540 ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic measurements (including alternating field demagnetization) on 16 oriented samples from five sites in the Precambrian anorthosite massif at Eger- sund, southern Norway, revealed a stable, consistent reversed remanent magnetiza- tion (after 150 oersted AF demagnetization, D = 315°, I = -82°, k = 92, a95 = 8°). The calculated paleomagnetic (south) pole lies at 42° N., 20° E. and is more than 45° from the pole (39° N., 40° W.) previously obtained from anorthosite of similar age at Allard Lake, Quebec. If Eurasia is fitted to North America accord- ing to the model of Bullard and others (1965), the rotated Egersund pole is at 42° N., 18° W. Allowing for the uncertainties in the data, this is not significantly different at the 5-percent level from the Allard Lake pole, and suggests that about 1,000 m.y. ago North America and Europe were contiguous as in Laurasian recon- structions. These results suggest that in the southern and western areas of the rift zone there has been substantial mag­ matism of pre-Kiaman age (i.e. pre ca. 300 m.y. B.P.). In pre­ Mesozoic times the areas of main igneous activity appear to have propagated northward. Thus, volcanic activity seems to have swept the Oslo district in the late Carboniferous and/or early Permian while in the northern extremity of the rift (at Brumunddal) out­ burst of lava flows took place in the latest Permian. The dolerites of the main part of the Sarv Nappe contain, after progressive alternating field and thermal demagnetization, a stable magnetic component of decl. 21.4". incl. -9.1". ass= 12.4'. k= 11.3. This gives a geomagnetic pole at lat. 21"N, long. 170"E which is in agreement with published Silurian-Devonian poles from Fennoscandia. This together with a simple 'fold test' implies that the Proterozoic dolerites became remagnetized during the Caledonian orogeny. The thermal demagnetization tests on the dolerites indicated a discrete blocking temperature inter- val of 550400°C. This is the temperature range in which the magnetization will be effectively fixed, and it is valid for the time the specimens were exposed to this temperature in the labora- tory test, ca. 300-1000 s. However, the effective blocking temperature will be considerably lowe- red during slow cooling. Considerations of the effects of slow cooling and thermal remanent magnetization (TRM) have been made by Pul- laiah et al. (1975), who showed that, theorFtica1- ly, the remanence in magnetite with blocking temperatures within 50°C of the Curie point can survive lower amphibolite facies metamorphism. However, in the same paper they presented ex- perimental data that were at variance with their theory and they concluded that very little, if any, remanence in magnetite can survive high green- schist facies metamorphism. This indicates the possibility of at least partial removal of the origi- nal TRhl in the dolerites and a build up of a new TRhl, or a possible chemical remanent magneti- zation (CRM) due to the formation of new mag- netic minerals. Generally the dif- ferences between the different methods were less than 2” and no systematic error was observed. The sampling sites are shown on the map(Fig. 1). For the measurements, one to four cylindrical specimens, 2.4 cm in height and 2.5 cm in diame- ter were obtained from each sample. The NRM was measured on a 85 Hz UGF-JR 3 or a 7 Hz Digico spinner magnetometer. Alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization techniques were used to remove unstable soft magnetization and to isolate the characteristic stable magnetic component. In both methods the demagnetiza- tion was done in fields of less than 10 nT. Pilot specimens from each site were step-wise de- magnetized to peak fields of 100 mT. Generally stable end-points for the magnetic vectors were obtained in the range 3040 mT, an exception being site SF for which a field of 80 mT was necessary to reach stability. After the pilot test the remaining specimens were demagnetized in five steps to 50 mT, and for site SF in eight steps to 100 mT. Thermal demagnetization was done in 13-14 steps to 600450°C on specimens from each site. All five samples from a site close to the western peak on mount Ottfjallet proved unsta- ble during progressive demagnetization and the results from this site were rejected. Palaeomagnetism has had its main success in establishing the presence of large-scale move- ments in the Earth's crust but the method is also applicable in many other fields such as the study of events in a period of orogeny. For example, the measurements of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), can give information about the magnetization build-up in relation to the metamorphic history of different units, in- cluding studies of relative movements. The Geotraverse, from Ostersund in Sweden across the Scandinavian Caledonides to Trondheim in Norway (Annersten 1973; Bylund et al. 1976) presents numerous possibilities for studies of this kind, and an obvious subject for such work is the well preserved parts of the Sarv Nappe with its conspicuous swarm of tholeiitic dolerite dykes. Palaeomagnetism has had its main success in establishing the presence of large-scale move- ments in the Earth's crust but the method is also applicable in many other fields such as the study of events in a period of orogeny. For example, the measurements of the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM), can give information about the magnetization build-up in relation to the metamorphic history of different units, in- cluding studies of relative movements. The resulting composite magnetization which may be of fairly high stability has proved difficult to split into its subcomponents and, therefore, palaeomag- netic figures can not be presented. In this novel extensional model, collapse of the footwall, i.e. the Mal~y Fault (Hossack 1984) or Nordfjord-Sogn detachment (Norton 1986), is considered to have led to sedimentary deposition in the hanging wall. Eastward onlap relationships originated as a roll-over anticline which accompanied the listric faulting. In Hossack’s model E-W folding and low-grade metamorph- ism of the Devonian sediments were produced as an accommodation to the lateral ramps produced by the presently observed marginal faults, with the implication of a syn-kinematic extensional origin for both deposition and deformation. The Kvamshesten and in part the Solund Massifs are undoubtedly floored by low-angle faults, but most likely of post-depositional origin (Torsvik et al. 1986, 1987b; Ramsay et al. 1987). The Devonian substrate in the Hornelen area indeed contains zones of mylonitic rocks (Brynhi 1964), but to date, no definitive geological evidence for a syn-depositional Devonian low-angle fault along the eastern margin has been documented. The area concerned is an area of geological complexity and has physical access problems. ly of post-depositional origin (Torsvik et al. 1986, 1987b; Ramsay et al. 1987). The Devonian substrate in the Hornelen area indeed contains zones of mylonitic rocks (Brynhi 1964), but to date, no definitive geological evidence for a syn-depositional Devonian low-angle fault along the eastern margin has been documented. The area concerned is an area of geological complexity and has physical access problems. At least part of the eastern margin is a surface of unconformity (Fig. 2), and any displacement was insufficient to produce significant mylonitization or destruction of well-preserved ORS weathering profiles in the substrate (Ramsay et al. 1987). The Hornelen Devonian sediments are assumed by most authors to have formed in an almost in situ basin where the original basin margins were approximately those seen today. In detail the pattern is more complex and the facies belts are sharply truncated by the northern and southern marginal faults. After the cooling the intensity and the direction of the re­ maining magnetization was measured. Thermal demagnetization is based on destroying the remanent magnetiza­ tion of particles with blocking temperatures lower than the selected heating temperature. In contrast to the alternating field demagnetizing method the thermal effects have no preferential direction. In the alternating field demagnetizing method, in which an alternating field of a certain strength is applied successively along three perpendicular axes, the maximum effect occurs in the domains with a magnetic moment directed parallel to the demagnetization axes. Because of several kinds of processes it is possible that the magnetic minerals obtain a Natural Remanent Magnitization (NRM) in a preferential direction. This preferential direction in the rocks often represents the geomagnetic field direction at the moment of rock formation. Two important tectonic lineaments intersect in Scania (SkAne), southernmost Sweden. One is the zone separating the Precambrian Fennoscan- dian Shield from central Europe and its sedimentary cover and the other is the Protogine Zone (PZ) which constitutes the border between the entirely different Proterozoic terrains of the southwestern and central Fennoscandian Shield. Movements and intrusions in these zones have contributed to the mosaic pattern and the mix of Proterozoic gneisses, granites and Phanerozoic sediments that form the geology of Scania. The purpose of this paper is to present a study of the magnetic properties of intrusive hyperite doler- ites and syenites from the Scanian part of the PZ in relation to their situation in the intersection between those tectonic lineaments. The Protogine Zone - other names sometimes used for this feature are the Schistosity Zone, The Gothide Front, the Svecononvegian Front - trends from Scania northwards across southern Sweden to Nonvay where it is cut by the Scan- dinavian Caledonides (Fig. 1). It separates the Svecononvegian southwestern corner of the Fennsocandian Shield from its central Sveco- karelian part. There is at present a running discussion whether the PZ is part of a global suture, the scar of a plate collision between a "Grenvillian-Svecononvegian" plate 'and the Laurentian-Fennoscandian plate or whether it is an intrashield structure along which movements have occurred intermittently during the Precam- brian, i.e. Donaldson et al. Component D is encountered on two sites only and is largely overprinted by the present Earth’s field. Individual flows are about 5 m thick and the total thickness is at least 600-800 m. The basalts consist of albitized plagioclase crystals, unaltered calcic augite, olivine more or less altered to serpentine, chlorite and hematite and smaller amounts of epidote, calcite, prehnite, pumpellyite and potash feldspar. The depositional environment is typi- cally subaerial. The primary textures of these rocks are relatively well preserved and a lack of penetra- tive deformation is also evident (Nixon and Pape- zik, 1979). G?OlOgy In the Colliers-Harbour Main and Bauline map-area (Fig. l), the Late Precambrian rocks of the Avalon zone are subdivided into three groups: (1) Harbour Main Group volcanic rocks, (2) Conception Group composed of voIcaniclastics, and (3) an upper sedimentary Group (Cabot Group) (Rose, 1952) which were renamed the St. Johns and Signal Hill Groups by Ring (1979). North of Colliers, these groups are overlain by Lower Paleozoic sedimentary units. The basic flows of group 1 investigated in this study are described as alkali basalts by Papezik (1970,1972). Magnetization Direction of M2 and M3 The igneous rocks (volcanics and diabase intrusions) of the Croteau and Seal Groups give evidence of two stable magnetic com- ponents. The stronger of these is directed at a moderate angle to the southeast; the weaker at a shallow angle to the west. The weaker west- erly-directed magnetization appears to be the later one because it is clearly related to the presence of hematite, throughout the rocks of some sites or within individual cores of less homogeneous sites. The hematitic nature of specimens carrying this component is indicated by redness, by a lower ferrous/ferric ratio in the rock as a whole (Table 3) and by the extreme resistance of these rocks to a.f. de- magnetization. In the volcanic rocks the hema- tization clearly postdates the consolidation of the flows as its presence is controlled by columnar joints, irregular fractures, or breccia zones. Similar evidence of hematization is al- most invariably reported in volcanic rocks of subaerial origin. In such rocks the hematization is generall

Further- more the Michael Gabbro shows no evidence of post-crystallization alteration and the Seal- Croteau rocks show only evidence of a late CRM (hematization), the effects of which have been greatly reduced. It is noteworthy in this regard that the Seal diabase which is least hematized exhibits a magnetization ( 143", +37") that most closely approaches that of the Michael Gabbro. Discussion The shift in pole position (50" of arc) be- tween the development of the igneous (TRM) and the later hematite (CRM) and the polarity reversal between the development of these magnetizations was a surprising element in this study. As noted above, the hematization of subaerial volcanic sequences is generally de- scribed as a late magmatic event. In the present case the hematization or the recrystallization of earlier hematite appears to have taken place significantly later than the original igneous activity. Two things suggest this, the very large shift of the paleomagnetic pole relative to this area of crust during the interval between the development of the TRM and the CRM, and the polarity reversal. section_candidates.excerpt: rocks of the Seal and Croteau were formed in the interval (~1200 to 2.1500 m.y. ago) during which time the paleomagnetic pole (relative to the Precambrian Shield of North America) was previously thought to have remained al- most stationary near the present-day equator (Palmer 1969, Spall 1971 ). Geology The Croteau and Seal Groups form an elon- gate belt of volcanic and sedimentary rocks that is preserved chiefly adjacent to, and north of the Grenville Front in Labrador (Fig. 1). The Croteau as defined (Fahrig 1959) consists of two parts, the lower being made up of black pyritic shales, graywacke, quartzite, dolomite, and metabasalt. This is overlain unconformably along Croteau and Pocket Knife Lakes by a basal conglomerate followed by sandstones. The latter is feldspathic and consists of alter- nating pink, maroon, and cream colored layers. Coarser phases of the sandstone are cross bedded and locally have a carbonate cement. The sandstones may be partly tuffaceous as devitrified shards are locally abundant. Above this basal zone the Croteau Group consists largely of intermediate to acid, purplish to green volcanic porphyries with thin layers of cross-bedded, tuffaceous cream to purple sand- stone. The above mentioned unconformity appears, however, to be

up names for the upper and lower sequences. In the present report the name Croteau will be restricted to the predominantly volcanic se- quence that lies above the unconformity. The Croteau Group thus defined, is Helikian in age, whereas the rocks below the unconformity may be significantly older, perhaps Aphebian in age. In the Snegamook Lake map area (Fahrig 1957, 1959, Brummer and Mann 1961) the strataform rocks of the Seal Group fall into five major lithostratigraphic units. The pre- dominant rock types of the five units, proceed- ing from the base of the group upward, are: (1) shales and coarse clastics, (2) volcanics and sandstones, (3) diabase with interlayered sandstone and shale, (4) volcanics and shale, and (5) sandstone. The presence of two separate volcanic sequences suggests cyclicity of igneous activity; however, the sedimentary rocks between the two volcanic sequences are extensively intruded by gabbro and diabase sills. It is conceivable that these intrusions are evidence of continuing igneous activity in the interval between the two periods of volcanism. Geology The Croteau and Seal Groups form an elon- gate belt of volcanic and sedimentary rocks that is preserved chiefly adjacent to, and north of the Grenville Front in Labrador (Fig. 1). The Croteau as defined (Fahrig 1959) consists of two parts, the lower being made up of black pyritic shales, graywacke, quartzite, dolomite, and metabasalt. This is overlain unconformably along Croteau and Pocket Knife Lakes by a basal conglomerate followed by sandstones. The latter is feldspathic and consists of alter- nating pink, maroon, and cream colored layers. Coarser phases of the sandstone are cross bedded and locally have a carbonate cement. The sandstones may be partly tuffaceous as devitrified shards are locally abundant. Above this basal zone the Croteau Group consists largely of intermediate to acid, purplish to green volcanic porphyries with thin layers of cross-bedded, tuffaceous cream to purple sand- stone. The above mentioned unconformity appears, however, to be

up names for the upper and lower sequences. In the present report the name Croteau will be restricted to the predominantly volcanic se- quence that lies above the unconformity. The Croteau Group thus defined, is Helikian in age, whereas the rocks below the unconformity may be significantly older, perhaps Aphebian in age. In the Snegamook Lake map area (Fahrig 1957, 1959, Brummer and Mann 1961) the strataform rocks of the Seal Group fall into five major lithostratigraphic units. The pre- dominant rock types of the five units, proceed- ing from the base of the group upward, are: (1) shales and coarse clastics, (2) volcanics and sandstones, (3) diabase with interlayered sandstone and shale, (4) volcanics and shale, and (5) sandstone. The presence of two separate volcanic sequences suggests cyclicity of igneous activity; however, the sedimentary rocks between the two volcanic sequences are extensively intruded by gabbro and diabase sills. It is conceivable that these intrusions are evidence of continuing igneous activity in the interval between the two periods of volcanism. As shown in figure 1, the Matachewan dikes are a swarm with a north-south strike. These are probably the oldest dikes, as they can be seen to be cut off by the younger flat-lying Precambrian rocks exposed in the portions of the shield near the Grenville Front. These younger flat-lying rocks are the Cobalt sedi- ments and the Nipissing diabase sill. The age of these flat-lying rocks is not yet fully agreed upon, but they are generally consid- ered to be about 1.5 billion years. Where the dikes have been carefully mapped, as for example in the Timmins area (Hogg, 1954), it is clear that there are man

An average inclination of - 100 falls within the circle of confidence of all the Matachewan north-south dikes. The use of the direction of remanent magnetism has thus enabled us to distinguish very definitely between the various dike swarms. In figure 4 a plot of declination versus in- clination is presented. In this figure the re- sults of Precambrian remanent-magnetism studies from the Lake Superior-Ontario- Quebec area are presented. It can readily be seen that a fairly smooth curve can be drawn through all the points. The flat-lying Ke- weenawan rocks in the vicinity of Lake Su- perior were reported by DuBois (1962), and data from the Sudbury Basin and basic in- trusives in the Grenville subprovince were reported by Hood (1958). These geologic units are in their correct time sequence. It is interesting to observe that the Duluth gabbro and some intrusives in the Grenville province (Boulter and Tu- dor gabbro-Hood, 1958) show similar di- rections of magnetization indicating an ap- proximate Keweenawan age for all these intrusives. Moving back along the curve, we find that the east-northeast dikes tend to fall in a group. This indicates that these dikes are probably pre-Keeweenawan in age although they have generally been classified as Keweenawan. It also indicates that these east-northeast dikes probably predate the Grenville orogeny by a short interval of time. The Grenville is commonly dated at 1,000 million years (Lowdon, 1961) or about the same as the Duluth gabbro dated at 1,120 million years (Goldich, Nier, Baads- gaard, Hoffman, and Krueger, 1961). The curve becomes rather indefinite at this point due to lack of data; but the Sud- bury (a) model of Hood shows that the di- rection of remanent magnetization in the Sudbury Basin and the east-northeast dikes is about the same, indicating a probable similar age for the two units. A single sam- ple from the Nipissing sill gives a direction which indicates a slightly older age. Detailed sampling of the Nipissing sill should help clarify the relationship with the Sudbury Basin and the east-northeast dikes. is presented. In Scotland the relative ages of the dikes could be determined with some accuracy by the strata they intruded. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. In the process of crystallization of diabasic magma it has been found that oli- vine and quartz are mutually exclusive, and it is supposed that the dikes of various com- positions are formed from different magmas. Unfortunately quartz and olivine are only present in small q

ime possible to classify dikes with any degree of certainty. The study of magnetic properties gives us another tool permitting a definite classification. DIKE SWARMS OF NORTHWEST QUEBEC AND NORTHEAST ONTARIO In the Precambrian Shield of Quebec and Ontario there are several well-developed dike swarms. In parts of the area, in partic- ular the commercially significant greenstone belts, detailed geologic mapping has been done. Recently, wide-scale aeromagnetic surveys have been carried out, showing the presence of a large number of dikes. In the present study a careful compilation of all reported dike exposures and all published airborne magnetic data of a portion of On- tario and Quebec has been made. In the maps accompanying this paper (figs. 1, 2) the compiled data are presented. It can be seen quite clearly that there are several dif- ferent dike swarms with different strike di- rections. is presented. In Scotland the relative ages of the dikes could be determined with some accuracy by the strata they intruded. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. In the process of crystallization of diabasic magma it has been found that oli- vine and quartz are mutually exclusive, and it is supposed that the dikes of various com- positions are formed from different magmas. It is shown that the direction of remanent magnetization, as well as the intensity, forms sepa- rate and distinct criteria for distinguishing between swarms. An earlier paper indicated that the direction of stable remanent magnetization is distorted by the shape of the dike. In spite of this distortion, widely differing directions of remanent magnetization indicate that the magnetic field of the earth existed in Precambrian times and that it wandered considerably in that era. From 16 sites, 197 specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal treatments to 710°C, and a further 46 to incremental af cleaning to 290 mT. The 10 sites from the unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite carry a magnetization with unblocking temperatures (TUB) generally between 600-625°C. with a significant fraction of remanence with TUB > 670°C. Similarly, most of the remanence has a resistive coercive force (rcf) of 100-175 mT, with a significant fraction exceed- ing 290 mT. The remanence is carried by two exsolution phases of titano-hematite, with the later and more hematite-rich lamellae having the higher TUB and rcf. Although only one direction exists, at two sites where intensities are somewhat lower and some natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) directions scattered, treatment reveals a dual polarity remanence. The pole (154"E, 02"s) obtained from these unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite sites falls on a well estab- lished segment of the late Precambrian apparent polar path of suitable age (~950 Ma). Significant results could not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treat

uld not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treatments. Data from two sites which display no shock effects and lie near the margin of the central uplift, and from one highly shocked sample from the crater centre show some possible effects of the shock event. All three have intensities substantially lower than in the St-Urbain sites, which is interpreted in the case of at least one of these sites as a shock-diminished remanence. A puzzling feature of the highly shocked samples is that the phase with a texture reminiscent of the ilmenite-hematite exsolution in the unshocked anorthosites, contains no iron. The remaining remanence, whose direction is parallel with that of the unshocked sites, is interpreted as pre- crater rather than shock-produced. Although many instances have been reported of a new shock-induced remanence imparted to rocks of equivalent and even lesser shock grade than those examined at Charlevoix, in all cases the magnetic carrier seems to have been magnetite. The lack of a shock-induced (emanence at Charlevoix is attributed to the high TUB and rcf of hematite in these rocks. well estab- lished segment of the late Precambrian apparent polar path of suitable age (~950 Ma). Significant results could not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treatments. Data from two sites which display no shock effects and lie near the margin of the central uplift, and from one highly shocked sample from the crater centre show some possible effects of the shock event. All three have intensities substantially lower than in the St-Urbain sites, which is interpreted in the case of at least one of these sites as a shock-diminished remanence. A puzzling feature of the highly shocked samples is that the phase with a texture reminiscent of the ilmenite-hematite exsolution in the unshocked anorthosites, contains no iron. The remaining remanence, whose direction is parallel with that of the unshocked sites, is interpreted as pre- crater rather than shock-produced. Earth Sci. 13,836846 (1976) Introduction This study is focussed on the paleomagnetism and geochemistry of the metabasalts and meta- gabbros of the northeastern portion of the Labrador geosyncline: More precisely, the area investigated is located in the Lac Patu (longitude: 69'00'-69' 15' W ; latitude : 56'30'-56'45' N) and Fort McKenzie areas (longitude : 68'30'-69'00' W; latitude: 56'45'-57'00' N). The objective of this paper is therefore twofold: firstly to obtain chemical, petrographic, and paleomagnetic data of the above-mentioned rock types; secondly, to derive their pole position from stability-tested data. Since paleomagnetism is becoming of greater importance in determining the time sequence of Precambrian rocks and in studying the nature of Precambrian orogenies, many additional paleomagnetic studies ought to be conducted in order to determine the variations of the Precambrian geomagnetic field. The volcanic rocks of the eugeosyncline (the eastern portion of the Trough) include some basalts, gabbros, rhyolites, tuffs, and ag- glomerates, with intercalations of sedimentary rocks (argillites, siltstones, and minor con- glomerates). All the volcanic rocks of the eugeosynclinal sector were included in the Montagnais Group by Dressler (1974), even though part of this volcanic sequence may be classified in the Murdoch Formation (Baragar 1967). Conformably above this, the Sayunei Formation is dominated by maroon to red, silty rhythmites with abundant dropstones. Conformably overlying this, the Shezal Formation successively comprises maroon and greenish grey mixtites. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: G.M. Yeo The Rapitan Group (sensu stricto) includes maroon and grey rnixtites, silty rhythmites, conglomerates, sandstones, and iron formation (Fig. 2.2). Maroon rhythmites of the Sayunei Formation are the basal unit over most of the Mountain River and Redstone River areas. In Thundercloud Range, however, mixtites underlie the Sayunei. Maroon rnixtites of the Snake River Tillite member of the Shezal Formation take the place of the Sayunei rhythmites in Snake River area. Maroon rnixtites of the Shezal Formation also locally overlie the Sayunei Formation. The upper Shezal Formation comprises mainly greenish grey mixtites. Jasper- hematite iron formation occurs in both the Shezal and Sayunei formations. Overyling the Rapitan Group are recessive, friable to fissile, dark grey shale and minor sandstone of the Twitya Formation. The Twitya interfingers with and is overlain by characteristically resistant carbonates, sandstones, and silt- stones of the Keele Formation. The Proterozoic succession is capped by recessive mudstones of the Sheepbed Formation. To emphasize their distinctness from the underlying clastics these three units have been collectively called the Hay Creek Group (Yeo, 1978; Young et al., 1979). Conformably above this lie resistant sandstones and carbon

mation is described in a later section. Siltstone-argillite Rhythmite Lithofacies The predominant lithofacies of the Sayunei Formation comprises millimetre to centimetre thick graded and laminated couplets of siltstone and argillite. Contacts between rhythrnites are typically knife-sharp and planar while contacts between the two size phases may be sharp or gradational. Recessive, calcareous siltstone and sandstone lenses and beds up to a few centimetres thick occur in the rhy thmites. Small -scale crosslamination may be preserved in such beds. The siliceous argillite phase of the rhythmite litho- facies is commonly so enriched in hematite towards the upper part of the Sayunei Formation as to be iron formation. Beds of jasper and hematite are commonly associated with such beds. Flame structures and load casts are common at the base of thick sandy rhythmites. Ripple crosslaminated sand beds and lenses up to several centimetres thick may be intercalated in the rhythmites. The rhythmites include Bouma AE, BCDE, CDE, and DE sequences. Hoffman (1979) has suggested that a recently recognized younger orogenic event in the Coronation Geosyncline may record a continental collision which juxtaposed the Great Bear batholith complex against the Hepburn Belt (Fig. 1.27). Hoffman has further speculated that this collisional event probably postdates the development of the Great Bear Batholith (1.7-1.9 Ga). The plate involved in this collisional event may be akin to one of the rnicroplates which Churkin and Eberlein (1977) have hypothesized were colliding with the western margin of the North American continent during the Proterozoic and Paleozoic. CONCLUSIONS The mid-Proterozoic Wernecke Supergroup is a 15 km- thick sequence of fine grained terrigenous and carbonate sediments which records a shoaling-upward miogeoclinal depositional regime. These strata constitute the oldest succession in the northern Cordillera and thus provide clues to the early geological evolution of this region. Analyses of paleocurrent data suggest that in the mid-Proterozoic, an east-west depositional margin lay to the north of the present day Wernecke Mountains. The origin of this depositional margin and the provenance of the sediments of the Wernecke Supergroup may be related to a continental collision event

In the latter case, checks were performed to avoid substantial errors due to strong local magnetization by sighting prominent topo- graphic features. The cores (diameter: 2.5 cm) each yielded at least two cylindrical specimens of nearly 2.5 cm in length. RESULTS OF THE MEASUREMENTS The direction and intensity of the remanent magnetiza- tion of the specimens from the volcanics were measured with an astatic magnetometer and those of the sediment samples with a spinner magnetometer with higher sensitivity. ins. The lowest unit, the Mount Berg Formation, is a grey-green mixtite seen only in the southern Mackenzie Mountains. Conformably above this, the Sayunei Formation is dominated by maroon to red, silty rhythmites with abundant dropstones. Conformably overlying this, the Shezal Formation successively comprises maroon and greenish grey mixtites. These two formations outcrop discontinuously throughout the southern and central Mackenzie Mountains. A homologous succession of rhythmites and mixtites is present in the Upper Tindir Group in Alaska. In the northern Mackenzie Mountains, however, only red and greenish grey mixtites occur. Jasper-hematite iron formation of probable rift-related, volcanogenic hydrothermal origin was found in the red mixtites of the northern Mackenzies as well as in the upper Sayunei and Tindir rhythmites. The Rapitan Group lies not far below the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary and overlies rocks judged to be about 0.8 Ga old. Except locally, the basal contact is distinctly unconformable. This unconf ormity marks the last major faulting event before the Paleozoic Era. The Proterozoic succession is capped by recessive mudstones of the Sheepbed Formation. Evans and Bingham (19731, incor- porating their paleomagnetic data with the published radiometric ages, suggested an age of 1730 + 1830 Ma for the Martin Formation. They also established that the hematitization preceded the folding, and thus must have taken place almost immediately after deposition. Paleocurrent measurements (Tremblay, 1972, Fig. 5) show that sediments in the Martin Lake Basin were derived from both sides of the basin and suggest that the basin was initially not significantly larger than at present. Iron Formation Lithofacies Laminated Iron Formation This is the predominant form of iron formation in Sayunei Formation. It is characterized by alternating laminae of hematite and jasper. Either component may dominate to form jasper-rich or hematite-rich bands and/or lenticular patches up to several centimetres thick. Contacts between the bands are generally sharp and even, coincident with lamination, but contacts between patchy areas are typically diffuse and irregular. Laminae may be traced continuously across their lateral contacts. Irregular hematite-rich patches within jasper-rich areas suggest local diagenetic iron enrichment. ins. The lowest unit, the Mount Berg Formation, is a grey-green mixtite seen only in the southern Mackenzie Mountains. Conformably above this, the Sayunei Formation is dominated by maroon to red, silty rhythmites with abundant dropstones. Conformably overlying this, the Shezal Formation successively comprises maroon and greenish grey mixtites. These two formations outcrop discontinuously throughout the southern and central Mackenzie Mountains. A homologous succession of rhythmites and mixtites is present in the Upper Tindir Group in Alaska. In the northern Mackenzie Mountains, however, only red and greenish grey mixtites occur. Jasper-hematite iron formation of probable rift-related, volcanogenic hydrothermal origin was found in the red mixtites of the northern Mackenzies as well as in the upper Sayunei and Tindir rhythmites. This unconf ormity marks the last major faulting event before the Paleozoic Era. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: G.M. Yeo The Rapitan Group (sensu stricto) includes maroon and grey rnixtites, silty rhythmites, conglomerates, sandstones, and iron formation (Fig. 2.2). Maroon rhythmites of the Sayunei Formation are the basal unit over most of the Mountain River and Redstone River areas. In Thundercloud Range, however, mixtites underlie the Sayunei. Maroon rnixtites of the Snake River Tillite member of the Shezal Formation take the place of the Sayunei rhythmites in Snake River area. Maroon rnixtites of the Shezal Formation also locally overlie the Sayunei Formation. The upper Shezal Formation comprises mainly greenish grey mixtites. Jasper- hematite iron formation occurs in both the Shezal and Sayunei formations. Overyling the Rapitan Group are recessive, friable to fissile, dark grey shale and minor sandstone of the Twitya Formation. The Twitya interfingers with and is overlain by characteristically resistant carbonates, sandstones, and silt- stones of the Keele Formation. The Proterozoic succession is capped by recessive mudstones of the Sheepbed Formation. To emphasize their distinctness from the underlying clastics these three units have been collectively called the Hay Creek Group (Yeo, 1978; Young et al., 1979). ins. The lowest unit, the Mount Berg Formation, is a grey-green mixtite seen only in the southern Mackenzie Mountains. Conformably above this, the Sayunei Formation is dominated by maroon to red, silty rhythmites with abundant dropstones. Conformably overlying this, the Shezal Formation successively comprises maroon and greenish grey mixtites. These two formations outcrop discontinuously throughout the southern and central Mackenzie Mountains. A homologous succession of rhythmites and mixtites is present in the Upper Tindir Group in Alaska. In the northern Mackenzie Mountains, however, only red and greenish grey mixtites occur. Jasper-hematite iron formation of probable rift-related, volcanogenic hydrothermal origin was found in the red mixtites of the northern Mackenzies as well as in the upper Sayunei and Tindir rhythmites. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: G.M. Yeo The Rapitan Group (sensu stricto) includes maroon and grey rnixtites, silty rhythmites, conglomerates, sandstones, and iron formation (Fig. 2.2). Maroon rhythmites of the Sayunei Formation are the basal unit over most of the Mountain River and Redstone River areas. In Thundercloud Range, however, mixtites underlie the Sayunei. Maroon rnixtites of the Snake River Tillite member of the Shezal Formation take the place of the Sayunei rhythmites in Snake River area. Maroon rnixtites of the Shezal Formation also locally overlie the Sayunei Formation. The upper Shezal Formation comprises mainly greenish grey mixtites. Jasper- hematite iron formation occurs in both the Shezal and Sayunei formations. Overyling the Rapitan Group are recessive, friable to fissile, dark grey shale and minor sandstone of the Twitya Formation. The Twitya interfingers with and is overlain by characteristically resistant carbonates, sandstones, and silt- stones of the Keele Formation. The Proterozoic succession is capped by recessive mudstones of the Sheepbed Formation. To emphasize their distinctness from the underlying clastics these three units have been collectively called the Hay Creek Group (Yeo, 1978; Young et al., 1979). Conformably above this lie resistant sandstones and carbon

mation is described in a later section. Siltstone-argillite Rhythmite Lithofacies The predominant lithofacies of the Sayunei Formation comprises millimetre to centimetre thick graded and laminated couplets of siltstone and argillite. Contacts between rhythrnites are typically knife-sharp and planar while contacts between the two size phases may be sharp or gradational. Recessive, calcareous siltstone and sandstone lenses and beds up to a few centimetres thick occur in the rhy thmites. Small -scale crosslamination may be preserved in such beds. The siliceous argillite phase of the rhythmite litho- facies is commonly so enriched in hematite towards the upper part of the Sayunei Formation as to be iron formation. Beds of jasper and hematite are commonly associated with such beds. Flame structures and load casts are common at the base of thick sandy rhythmites. Ripple crosslaminated sand beds and lenses up to several centimetres thick may be intercalated in the rhythmites. The rhythmites include Bouma AE, BCDE, CDE, and DE sequences. Complete Bouma sequences are rare. Convolute bedding is locally well developed (Young, 1976, Plate lb). Coarse grained, sandy, clastic dykes are also found locally. Hoffman (1979) has suggested that a recently recognized younger orogenic event in the Coronation Geosyncline may record a continental collision which juxtaposed the Great Bear batholith complex against the Hepburn Belt (Fig. 1.27). Hoffman has further speculated that this collisional event probably postdates the development of the Great Bear Batholith (1.7-1.9 Ga). The plate involved in this collisional event may be akin to one of the rnicroplates which Churkin and Eberlein (1977) have hypothesized were colliding with the western margin of the North American continent during the Proterozoic and Paleozoic. CONCLUSIONS The mid-Proterozoic Wernecke Supergroup is a 15 km- thick sequence of fine grained terrigenous and carbonate sediments which records a shoaling-upward miogeoclinal depositional regime. These strata constitute the oldest succession in the northern Cordillera and thus provide clues to the early geological evolution of this region. Analyses of paleocurrent data suggest that in the mid-Proterozoic, an east-west depositional margin lay to the north of the present day Wernecke Mountains. The origin of this depositional margin and the provenance of the sediments of the Wernecke Supergroup may be related to a continental collision event

section_candidates.excerpt: In situ "primary" magnetization data from Kinojevis and older units should be corrected for structure because lava successions have been tilted into monoclinal sequences well after emplacement and original cooling. The data presented here and in companion papers (Tasillo-Hirt et al. 1982; Geissman et al. 1982, and in preparation) are results of our efforts to extract further information on the Archean field from units of the Abitibi Greenstone Belt. We assumed that an original, syngenetic component of magnetization of statistical significance was present in the lithologies examined, and tests are applied for the presence of this remanence in as many instances as possible. Methodology Samples were collected by field drilling techniques or by orienting blocks. A magnetic compass was used for orientation (accuracy of 1-2"). Generally, two to five specimens (2.5 cm long by 2.5 cm diameter) were prepared from each core or block sample. Details of the sampled areas are given with the paleomagnetic data. The remanent magnetization was generally measured with the prototype SCT rock magnetometer (Goree and Fuller 1976) having a 4 in. GEOLOGICAL FEATURES All of the four iron formation deposits are Archean BIF of the magnetite oxide facies with three located in the Abitibi Belt and one in the Uchi Belt of the Superior Province in the Canadian Shield. The BIF horizons range in thickness from -50 to -150 m and are interlayered with siliceous metasediments associated with Archean metavolcanics of basic to acidic composition. These strata were deformed during the Kenoran Orogeny at -2.55 Ga at which time minor basic and large acidic plutons were emplaced adjacent to or within a few kilometers of the deposits. Thus the HR contribution to the residual anomaly may be neglected. The NRM for the IF augments the calculated anomaly intensity by 14%. Combining the AMS and NRM augmenting effects with a demagnetizing factor of 2 77, yields theoretical anomaly calculations for the North and South Pit deposits that are within 10% of the measured anomalies in terms of peak intensity and half -width. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at ^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at ~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the 20 Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between the two events. Given the large variety of attitudes of the BIF in these deposits, the NAF represents a reasonable value regardless of the attitude of a given BIF. The NAF represents the swing of viscous remanence components (VRM) into alignment with the EMF, and thus has the effect of increasing the induced magnetization regardless of the attitude of the BIF. Thus the HR contribution to the residual anomaly may be neglected. The NRM for the IF augments the calculated anomaly intensity by 14%. Combining the AMS and NRM augmenting effects with a demagnetizing factor of 2 77, yields theoretical anomaly calculations for the North and South Pit deposits that are within 10% of the measured anomalies in terms of peak intensity and half -width. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at ^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at ~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the 20 Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between the two events. Stupavsky Department of Geology, University of Windsor Windsor, Ontario, N9B 3P4 INTRODUCTION This study was performed as four related but separate studies of Algoman-type banded iron formations (BIF) in Ontario. The results of the study for the Sherman Mine near Temagami have been reported in full by Symons and Stupavsky (1979,1980), for the Moose Mountain Mine near Capreol by Symons et al (1980), for the Adams Mine near Kirkland Lake by Symons et al (1981), and for the Griffiths Mine near Red Lake by Symons et al (1982). The latter study forms the second article in this Open File Report. The purpose of this article is to summarize the results of the four studies primarily in tabular form with relevant comments. Natural Remanent Magnetization The NAF for the NRM of the four deposits is 0.19. or 19%. Given the large variety of attitudes of the BIF in these deposits, the NAF represents a reasonable value regardless of the attitude of a given BIF. The NAF represents the swing of viscous remanence components (VRM) into alignment with the EMF, and thus has the effect of increasing the induced magnetization regardless of the attitude of the BIF. The presence of significant VRM components is well documented from alternating field (AF) demagnetization, thermal (Th) demagnetization, and VRM decay tests such as storage and shock tests. The hard remanence components cannot be calculated in general terms unless the specific orientation of their vectors and their magnitudes are known. The mean natural remanent magnetization (NRM) 2 5 -3 intensities for the IF and HR are 2.1 x 10 and 1.47 x 10 emu cm which give mean Koenigsberger ratios of 0.66 and 0.051 respectively. Thus the HR contribution to the residual anomaly may be neglected. The NRM for the IF augments the calculated anomaly intensity by 14%. Combining the AMS and NRM augmenting effects with a demagnetizing factor of 2 77, yields theoretical anomaly calculations for the North and South Pit deposits that are within 10% of the measured anomalies in terms of peak intensity and half -width. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at ^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at ~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the 20 Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between the two events. INTRODUCTION Paleomagnetism can be used to determine the genesis of some iron ore deposits by comparing the remanence direction of the ore deposit with that of the host rock or of other rocks of known age from the same geologic pro- vince, and by determining whether the remanence of the ore deposit was acquired before or after folding. Thus a syngenetic deposit has a prefolding remanence which it acquired during the time interval between deposition of the enclosing rock formations. By this method, Gross and Strangway (1961) concluded that the "deep hard hematite" deposit at F'Derik in Mauritania is a Precambrian syngenetic deposit and that the "surficial hard hematite" deposit at Rouessa West is a Cenozoic laterite. Similarly, DuBois (1961, 1962) demonstrated that a hard hematite deposit in Cumberland, England, is an epigenetic deposit of Permian-Triassic age in host rocks of Lower Carboni- ferous age. In this study, paleomagnetism is used to study the genesis of the hard hematite ore of the Cliff-Shaft mine, Marquette Iron Range, Michigan, U.S.A., and of the hard goethite ore of the Caland and Steep Rock mines, Steep Rock Iron Range, Ontario, Canada. INTRODUCTION Paleomagnetism can be used to determine the genesis of some iron ore deposits by comparing the remanence direction of the ore deposit with that of the host rock or of other rocks of known age from the same geologic pro- vince, and by determining whether the remanence of the ore deposit was acquired before or after folding. Thus a syngenetic deposit has a prefolding remanence which it acquired during the time interval between deposition of the enclosing rock formations. sediments were laid down in this basin, but were followed by enormous outpourings of lava. Basic lavas welled up quietly from fissures in the centre of the syncline, filled it, and overflowed to the borders of the syncline. The more acidic lavas being very viscous formed hummock-like hills, which were eroded to form boulders in the conglomerates interbedded with, and overlying the lavas. The extrusive phase ceased and downwarping continued. Already active thrust faults raised the lavas along the margins of the syncline, thus exposing them to erosion. The detritus from the lavas and the adjacent pre-Keweenawan rocks was carried by streams and deposited in the syncline. Studies of current crossbedding show that the streams flowed from the margins towards the centre of the syncline. Sedimentation kept pace with the downwarping and the surface of the syncline was always shallow as indicated by the ripple-marks, mud-cracks, rain-drop imprints, and the well-oxidized condition of the sediments. During the process of sedimentation and volcanic extrusion, basic intrusions such as the Duluth gabbro were emplaced. It is thought that :the main activity of this fault was during Keweenawan time, but as the Jacobsville sandstone, which is on the eastern (footwall) side of the fault, has been crumpled along their mutual contact there must have been some movement in post-Jacobsville time. Some smaller faults, principally tear faults, were observed cutting the trap obliquely to the strike of the lava flows, but they are relatively unimportant. Southeast of the Keweenaw fault the fiat-lying Jacobsville sandstone consists principally of fine-grained , red, buff, and white sandstones. The red sandstone contains white spots, where evidently the hematite, which gives the rock its dis­ tinctive colour, has been reduced perhaps by the presence of organic material. The base of the Jacobsville is not visible on the peninsula, but farther to the southea st near L'Anse it is observed to rest on folded Animikie-type rocks . Northern Wisconsin Formations of the Keweenaw Peninsula can in general be projected to the southwest along strike towards the Michigan-Wisconsin boundary . The lavas and overlying sediments dip towards the lake and are cut off to the east by a large thrust fault. To the east of this fault are fiat-lying Jacobsville sandstones. Near Gogebic Lake a branch of the Keweenawan

reddish grey sandstone overlie the lavas with considerable unconformity . These sandstones generally have a dip of 15 degrees. Along the south shore of Batchawana Bay the author found an area of highly disturbed sandstone , pre­ sumably the result of faulting . In appearance these rocks are much like the Freda sandstones of Michigan. The second type of sandstone is exposed around Sault Ste. Marie, in the valley of St. Mary's River. This sandstone is much more irregularly bedded, poorly sorted, and poorly consolidated than that of the first type. It is a lso characterized by a much redder colour with white spots and layers , where the hematite appears to have been bleached. Its physical appear­ ance closely resembles the J acobsville sandstone. This sandstone also appears to be much more extensive and thicker than the sandstones of the first type. Finally, it appears everywhere to be nearly flat lying and undisturbed. McConnell (1927) lumped these sandstones together into one group which he called the Lake Superior sandstone. However, Hamblin (19 5 8) recently sug­ gested that the first type of sandstone should be correlated with the Freda and has shown that the second type, exposed at Sault Ste. Marie and around White­ fish Bay, is an eastward extension of the Jacobsville sa

Most of the massive lava is exceedingly fresh and shows few signs of altera­ tion and metamorphism after solidification. Butler, et al. (1929) showed that the principal alterations, aside from copper ore deposition and surface weathering, occurred in the magnetite and olivine, the pyroxene and feldspar generally being unaffected . The olivine, which at the time of crystallization was common in many of the lavas, is rarely preserved and has been replaced by serpentine and hematite . Similarly, the magnetite has been altered more or less completely to hematite. In cases where hematite has replaced magnetite completely, irregular stringers of hematite extend from the magnetite grain among the surrounding minerals . This suggests that in the alteration of magnetite a volume increase forced some of the hematite to lodge outside the original boundary of the magnetite. Some of the magnetite was evidently titaniferous, for its alteration has produced numerous granular particles of a non-metallic mineral, probably titanite, as well as the more abundant hematite. Magnetic Washing Many samples of rock collected for palaeomagnetic research have remanent magnetic moments that do not form a consistent pattern when first measured. A detailed study of shatter cones on the Slate Islands has now been completed (Stesky & Halls 1978) and shows that they are abundantly developed throughout the islands although restricted to certain rock types. The majority of cones point inwards and upwards, toward the centre of Patterson Island. A detailed study of shatter cones on the Slate Islands has now been completed (Stesky & Halls 1978) and shows that they are abundantly developed throughout the islands although restricted to certain rock types. The majority of cones point inwards and upwards, toward the centre of Patterson Island. The central location of the shock origin with respect to the Slate Island group, originally estimated from only four sites (Halls & Grieve 1976) is now confirmed. A summary of this new shatter cone data will be presented later with the palaeomagnetic results. Estimated shock levels based on deformation lamellae support a centrally located shock point as they vary from about 60 kb along the SW coast of Patterson Island to about 150 kb a further 2 km inland (Grieve & Robertson 1976).
