directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: Matachewan swarm, trends north to northwest and is composed of quartz tholeiite dykes that are found in virtually every part of a 500 km wide swath of Archean shield that borders Lake Superior to the east and northeast. These dykes have been documented, mainly through paleomagnetic studies, in the Abitibi Belt (e.g., Strangway 1964; Pesonen 1973; Buchan and Schwarz 1981; Condie et al. 1987) and also in a region extending from Hearst to Wawa on the western side of the KSZ (Ernst and Halls 1984). Matache- wan dykes are recognized in the field by the presence of pale green feldspar phenocrysts and in the laboratory by a dual magnetic polarity (declination: D = 30"/210° ; inclination: I = +lo0/-10"). Their paleomagnetic signature is unique amongst Canadian Shield dykes and serves to distinguish them, especially where they lack phenocrysts, from dykes of younger swarms. Although many of the dykes shown in Fig. 2 are likely to be Matachewan, others of similar trend, but belonging to three younger groups, may be present. North of the Huronian fold belt (HFB in Fig. 1) in the Elliot Lake area, Aibangbee (1982) mapped northwest-trending quartz diabase dykes that both predate and postdate the basal Huronian sedimentary units. The pre-Huronian dykes give typical Matachewan pal

ture. Demagnetization and magnetometer measurements were terminated for each specimen when the field limit of the demagnetizer (100 mT) was reached or when remanence directions and intensities began to scatter. Specimen demagne- tization data were analyzed using methods described by Halls (1986). Paleomagnetic results On the basis of characteristic components of magnetization, lithology, and petrography, the dykes were divided into four main age groups corresponding to the Matachewan, Preissac NW, Sudbury , and Keweenawan swarms (Appendix). Within the Matachewan and Preissac NW swarms, dykes of both nor- mal and reversed magnetic polarity were found. Details of specimen demagnetization behaviour and petrography were given by Shaw (1985). Matachewan dykes are by far the most numerous. Lithologically, they are quartz diabases, often con- taining the diagnostic green plagioclase phenocrysts. In gen- eral, they are moderately to heavily altered (50-80%), with groundmass plagioclase replaced by sausserite and chlorite, and pyroxene extensively uralitized, especially around the margins. Nipissing diabase intrusions consist mainly of pyroxene gabbro and hornblende gabbro, but differentiation has led to the formation of minor amounts of feldspathic pyroxenite, gabbroic anorthosite, and granophyre. Olivine is present in several intrusions in the Cobalt and Englehart areas but the typical mafic minerals are augite, hypersthene, hornblende, and minor biotite. Calcic plagioclase, quartz, sulphides, iron - titanium oxides (ilmenite - titaniferous magnetite and ilmenite -hematite), and minor apatite form the remainder. Major- and minor-element chemistry indicates that all of these rocks formed from magma of similar composition with differ- entiation mainly by gravitative settling of early-formed mafic minerals with consequent depletion of residual liquids in Mg and Ca and enrichment in iron and alkalis. Alteration of the Nipissing Diabase, whether by low-grade regional metamorphism as in the Sudbury area (Card 1978) or by deuteric alteration as in the Cobalt area, resulted in replace- ment of the primary minerals by uralitic amphiboles, albite, epidote, chlorite, and quartz or quartz -feldspar intergrowths. The primary ilmenite - magnetite and ilmenite - hematite intergrowths are replaced by magnetite - sphene - leucoxene aggregates. In addition, uralitization of the mafic minerals commonly results in formation of fine-grained oxides and sul- phides. Perhaps the grey sediments of this area were not stably magnetized before Nipissing intrusion, but chemical alterations at the time of intrusion produced magnetic minerals capable of carrying a stable remanence in sediments adjacent to the sill (i.e., site 8512). Major- and minor-element chemistry indicates that all of these rocks formed from magma of similar composition with differ- entiation mainly by gravitative settling of early-formed mafic minerals with consequent depletion of residual liquids in Mg and Ca and enrichment in iron and alkalis. Alteration of the Nipissing Diabase, whether by low-grade regional metamorphism as in the Sudbury area (Card 1978) or by deuteric alteration as in the Cobalt area, resulted in replace- ment of the primary minerals by uralitic amphiboles, albite, epidote, chlorite, and quartz or quartz -feldspar intergrowths. The primary ilmenite - magnetite and ilmenite - hematite intergrowths are replaced by magnetite - sphene - leucoxene aggregates. In addition, uralitization of the mafic minerals commonly results in formation of fine-grained oxides and sul- phides. Also cutting the Huronian rocks are northeast-trending quartz diabase dykes of the Preissac swarm with an 40Ar- 39Ar isotopic age of 2150 Ma (Hanes and York 1979) and younger northeast trending olivine diabase dykes of the Abitibi swarm with a U-Pb baddeleyite age of 1140 Ma (Krogh et al. 1987). PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. None of the previous paleo­ magnetic interpretations can yet be disputed or corroborated in the light of the above analysis but their basis and the planning of future work to test them is undoubtedly established more firmly. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. None of the previous paleo­ magnetic interpretations can yet be disputed or corroborated in the light of the above analysis but their basis and the planning of future work to test them is undoubtedly established more firmly. This sandstone and shale is the Nonesuch, wtfich, with the overlying Freda, consists of fine grained reddish or purplish grey sandstone, silt~tone and shale. The Jacobsville is mainly a fine to medium grained sandstone, brick red in colour except for many white spots where evidently reduction of red haematite has taken place. The Chequamegon is a medium to coarse grained sandstone, which is the stratigraphically highest Keweenawan formation to be found.
